utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries, are there, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to note the Chamber might be expecting an oral argument on exhibits related to two recent witnesses. Mr. Lukic informed us this morning that he had filed written submissions this morning, so rather than orally respond we'll do that in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be a very practical approach to the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this time the Prosecution will call Ekrem Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I put on the record the following: On the 22nd of November of last year, the Defence requested an extension of the response time for the Rule 92 ter motion in relation to Witness Ekrem Suljevic. On the 23rd of November, the Prosecution responded disagreeing with the facts set out in the request but not opposing the brief extension. On the 26th of November, the Chamber through an informal communication granted an extension until the 30th of November. And that decision is hereby, although rather late, put on the record. I take it, Mr. Weber, that the Prosecution requests for leave to amend the 65 ter list, add two new photographs, will be dealt with when you come to those photographs, or would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was planning on addressing it when I called up the photographs. And also the Prosecution sought leave to amend 65 ter 19024 and we'll also address that when we come to that exhibit, if it's okay with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be the best way to approach the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, I would like to invite you to make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out you to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Suljevic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Ekrem Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, have you previously testified before this Tribunal on three earlier occasions in the Dragomir Milosevic, Perisic, and Karadzic cases?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Prior to your testimony in the Karadzic case, did you provide a consolidated statement containing information from your previous testimony and statements?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 28668.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document before you as the amalgamated statement you provided on 9 February 2010?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does your signature appear in the middle portion of this page?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to review this statement in the Bosnian language prior to court today?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During your testimony in the Karadzic case, did you make corrections to this statement?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the Chamber's leave, and I've also discussed this matter with Mr. Lukic, the Prosecution would read the previous corrections and ask the witness to confirm them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Lukic agrees, the Chamber does not object. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, having reviewed this statement again for this case, would you still make the following corrections: In paragraph 1, the reference to Stanislav Galic should be replaced by Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 8, line 2, the words "Mirza Jamakovic" should come after the words "the chief of our department," in the next sentence?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 17, line 5, the words "and the flight" should be deleted.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the same paragraph on line 7, the words "the location from which the projectile had been fired" should be inserted after the word "observed." It's in the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 48, on two occasions the word "shell" appears. This word should be changed to "primary charge."

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the heading before paragraph 49, the date should read "24th of May" not "26th of May."

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As a general point of clarification before we return to the statement, when you refer to primary charge, what part of the mortar are you discussing?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The primary charge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, does it make sense to -- to work on a redacted portion of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just was clarifying it since it was part of the statement. I'm not intending to lead any evidence related to those events on the 24th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this is how it looks. How could I -- it's a redacted portion of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It was just the heading that I was seeking to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The heading. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Which I believe is still unredacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. The heading is -- let me just check. You said paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Above paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before paragraph 48. Yes. That should be?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness confirmed that it should be the 24th of May, not the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So now we know what day everything happened, which we do not know that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's certainly -- that's certainly assisting. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, I just wanted to -- since one of your clarifications related to the use of the word "primary charge," I was just asking you to indicate what part of the mortar you're discussing when you say "primary charge."

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is primary charge and not a mortar but, rather, a projectile for mortar. The primary charge is on the lower side of the stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you have any additional clarifications or corrections to this statement?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think there is any need to add anything. These were simply technical modifications or mistranslations or other mistakes as was the case with the change of using the name Galic instead of Milosevic, which is another technical error.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please have page 12 of the English version and page 22 of the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When this appears before you, Mr. Suljevic, could you please review the last page of the statement and verify whether you signed this page.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions, would you provide the same answers in substance as you did in this statement?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now that you've taken the solemn declaration in this case, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders the 2010 statement uploaded under 65 ter 28668 into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28668 receives number P889, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P889 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has provided a list of associated exhibits to the Chamber today. We've also provided a copy of this list to the Defence and the Registry. With your leave today, the Prosecution is respectfully requesting a departure from the Chamber's guidance on the number of associated exhibits due to the witness's authentication of documentation of the BiH MUP and comments in a comment chart on a number of materials related to munitions used by the VRS. In the list there are two sections. The first section corresponds to the associated exhibits being tendered from the amalgamated statement just admitted as P889. In total there were 24 associated exhibits to the statement. One exhibit has already been admitted as part of P495. At this time, the Prosecution tenders 15 of the remaining exhibits which are official BiH MUP reports related to investigations of projectile impacts between May and July 1995. After addressing these exhibits the Prosecution has additional questions for the witness with respect to a second chart containing comments on the remaining exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you want to respond at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think I can, that actually we do not object to three documents from this list, and those are documents composed or signed by the witness. Those are -- if you have the newest list from Mr. Weber, that's documents under numbers 6, 9, and 12. On the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first page, documents 6, 9, and 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 13, sorry -- no, no, 12. We do not have objections to those three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is, just for me, 65 ter 10157.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. No. The 13 is out, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thirteen is out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. No objections against those three, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the others?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the others we do object, Your Honour, since this gentleman did not take part in either composing those documents and we don't see that he took any part in the work preceding the composition of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it is unrelated to the testimony of this witness, because not being the author and not participating in itself may not be a sufficient reason to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe he will -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we first hear the testimony of the witness and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and then we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do believe that these are properly admitted through this witness as associated exhibits. He did authenticate them as being reports he recognised from the BiH MUP and also provided his knowledge with respect to what's in there, and I'm happy to discuss this further with Mr. Lukic and see what we can resolve during the course of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll first hear what the witness says about it, although we can read, of course, part of it already in this statement. That is the first portion. The second portion is of a different nature --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to Mr. Lukic, do you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have further questions for the witness before I tender those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we, then, leave that also until when we have heard the evidence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just want to inform the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- that we do object to admission of all those documents through this witness since he has no knowledge about the documents at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it seems that the Prosecution leaves an admission from the bar table as an option.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's different issue. Then we'll address it when it's bar tabled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes if documents are in a close relationship with the testimony of a witness, we then deviate from our practice that we would like to have all the bar table documents at a later stage. So could you then also consider whether, in the present circumstances, whether you would object against admission at this stage of the proceedings. So apart from any objection as far as content is concerned. We'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of 65 ter 28669. Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of 65 ter 28669.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, do you recognise the document before you as a chart of comments you provided on 19 July 2010, prior to your testimony in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the top of this page, you state that these documents concern air bombs and other projectiles. There are then also cross-references to paragraphs of your amalgamated statement which was just admitted. My question for you: Are your comments on this chart based upon the experience you acquired during investigations into the types of projectiles used in shellings of Sarajevo, including modified air bombs, mortars, and artillery?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, based on experience and on the teamwork conducted during investigations that were carried out at the request of all the traces that were submitted for expert analysis after being collected in situ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In each of your comments on this chart, did you note the equipment or munitions you are familiar with from your investigations of traces of projectiles during the war?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you again review this chart and the associated documents prior to your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you have any corrections or clarifications to your comments in this chart?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking there are no major observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you were asked questions about the documents listed in the chart, would you make the same comments about these materials?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28669, the chart of comments. The Prosecution also can address the 39 non -- yet not admitted exhibits related to this chart. The Prosecution recognises that the witness is not the author of any of these documents and his comments in this chart are based on his knowledge as he's indicate the just now. Based on that, we are tendering it pursuant to Rule 89(C) from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would you like to respond now? Would you prefer to take more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we should take more time, but in general we do object to admission of this chart, because there's only reading the document and saying, yes, that type of ammunition was used. So there is three -- two, three types of ammunition used in that conflict in total, so we are not gaining anything from having 39 documents to learn that there is 82-millimetre mortar shell was used in that conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you agreed on the use of 82-millimetre mortar being used, because that's what you're suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the conflict, yes. It was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, these documents indicate much more than that, and if I could give an example and there are things that are -- that the Prosecution recognises that are beyond the witness's direct knowledge. The first document, 65 ter 8768, is a document from the director of the Pretis holding company dated 10 May 1994 to the Main Staff of the VRS personally to the accused, and this references 1.000 GRAD 122-millimetre rockets. It does have a nexus to the witness's evidence in the context of the fact that on, as an example, page 9 of P495, the witness authors a report concerning scheduled incident G13, where the witness concludes the same type of rockets -- rocket engines were used and found at the location of the projectile impact. The witness further comments on this type of rocket engine in paragraph 53 of his amalgamated statement. So we're offering it in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided that it will reserve 40 numbers for these 40 documents, that's the chart and the 39 underlying documents, and invites the parties -- Mr. Lukic, there seems to be disagreement as to what exactly the chart and the comment of the witness brings us. Therefore, the parties are invited perhaps also in a chart format to bring to the attention of the Chamber, you, Mr. Weber, what favours admission, and you, Mr. Lukic, what does object admission. And of course, for Mr. Weber, there's no need to repeat what is already in the chart itself, and I think the simplest way would be that the Defence first formulates its objections and that the Prosecution then further specifies the reason why it seeks admission of those specific documents. Could the parties agree on a kind of a schedule for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be happy today to provide Mr. Lukic with a Word version of a chart for him to provide comments on the individual documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would that be a practical way of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is very, Your Honour, only I don't know if the numbers in this chart are from Karadzic trial. So it can create confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says "Mladic 65 ter numbers," but is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On the chart -- on the chart distributed to the Chamber and to the Defence today those are the Mladic 65 ter numbers. I'm happy to include in the chart that I provide to Mr. Lukic today the corresponding Karadzic numbers, just so when he reviews the comment chart he can --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I was referring to this second statement from the 19th of July, 2010. We have old numbers from Karadzic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is correct that in the comment chart itself those are -- that appear in the far left column, those are the Karadzic 65 ter numbers. We have attached a table of concordance and I can also provide in the chart today, in the Word version, both the 65 ter numbers so he can easily go through them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would prepare a chart for Mr. Lukic so that he always has the two numbers in two columns available to himself. Mr. Lukic, rather than to change what seems to be a document where the witness commented on certain matters, rather not change anything in that and have the conversion chart for you available.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll proceed. Madam Registrar, the numbers to be reserved for these purposes are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The numbers reserved exclusively deal with the chart and the underlying documents of the chart. All the -- I would say the section 1 associated exhibits is not covered by that yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I proceed with the summary of the witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. We'll first ask Madam Registrar to tell us which numbers she reserved.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 40 numbers reserved are from number P890 up to and including P929, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those numbers are reserved. Please proceed, Mr. Weber, and read the summary of the statement of the witness and you have explained to the witness what the purpose of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And for the public, we'll now read the summary of the statement of the witness which is the core of the evidence the witness has given although not viva voce today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Ekrem Suljevic is a mechanical engineer and was an investigator for the Counter Sabotage Protection Unit, or KDZ, of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Suljevic participated in 50 to 60 investigations of shelling incidents at civilian locations during the siege of Sarajevo. One of the first investigations the witness worked on was the Markale I shelling. In his amalgamated statement, Mr. Suljevic discusses reports by the RBiH MUP KDZ and the Sarajevo CSB related to shelling or modified air bomb impacts in Sarajevo between May and July 1995. The witness explains the methodology of the RBiH MUP when investigating shelling incidents, including determining the direction of fire and the collection and analysis of projectile fragments. Mr. Suljevic further explains his familiarity with components and manufacturer markings of various projectiles, including markings found on mortar stabilisers which indicate the year in which they were manufactured and the location of manufacture, which in many cases was the Krusik factory in Valjevo, Serbia. Mr. Suljevic also discusses the components of modified air bombs. This completes the summary of the witness, and, Your Honours, may I proceed with questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, in paragraph 7 of your amalgamated statement, P889, you state: "The kinds of projectiles whose craters we inspected were mortar shells, artillery gun shells such as howitzer shells, and modified air bombs." During the course of these inspections, did you personally become familiar with the crater patterns caused by both mortar and artillery shells?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is there a difference in the appearance of an impression or a crater that would be left by a mortar shell as compared to an artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is a difference between a crater created by a mortar shell and a crater caused by some other type of weaponry. There is also a difference between a crater created by an air bomb which explodes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll discuss the differences at greater length in a second, but before doing that, I'd like to ask you do you know why a mortar shell leaves a distinguishable crater pattern from that of an artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's put it very simply. There are several distinguishing traits, starting with the shape of the shell, the way the shell flies, and the way the projectile is stabilised, because mortar shells do not rotate during flight. They are stabilised by stabiliser, whereas shells from other artillery pieces such as cannons and howitzers rotate, and their rotation provides them with the necessary flight stabilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you for a second. Mr. Weber didn't ask for all the differences between the two projectiles and how they are functioning or flying but was specifically asking about the pattern on the ground upon impact. May I invite you, unless it is necessary to understand that, to start with that first. What do you see on the ground upon impact? Mr. Weber, that's what you asked, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you didn't, then rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are the distinguishing traits that you've just mentioned in your answer, do these affect the crater pattern that is left on the ground?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I'd ask that the witness be provided with a pen and a blank screen to draw upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be -- Mr. Weber, my colleague just reminds me that your question was not about what the differences are on the ground but why they left that. So I misread your question. My apologies for that. And the witness may be provided with a pen and a blank screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, I'd first like to discuss mortars with you. On the screen before you, could you please draw how a mortar impacts and explodes on a horizontal surface such as the ground.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try and do it from what I remember. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If -- before you continue with your drawing, could you please explain to us what you have drawn. It appears to be a mortar, and you've drawn a number of lines. If you could please explain these to us.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just briefly. The drawing depicts a mortar shell on impact with a horizontal surface, and the lines represent actually from the centre of explosion, and every part of the shell body, i.e., every fragment moves in the direction of these lines. This is just a simplified representation. Most of the shell fragments will hit the surface on the side from which the shell was launched. On the other side there will be less fragment impact, and those fragments will form a rose-shaped pattern or a paw pattern as we used to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to how mortars -- their angle of descent, does this impact how the pattern is created at all?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: It does. I will repeat that I did not carry out analysis and calculations of angles of descent, but the angle of descent does define the crater pattern, and later, based on calculations, you can also calculate the angle of descent at the moment of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You began to draw a line in the middle of this page. I was wondering if on the right of this line, if you could draw what you've described to be the rose-shaped or paw pattern that is created by the mortar.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Marks]. Generally speaking, that would be the shape. In the centre is the crater centre, and around it are non-symmetrical shapes elongated towards the opposite side from the side from which the shell came. A more dense pattern on the surface, i.e., a smaller distance between the rings can be seen on the side from which the projectile came. Generally speaking, the pattern is symmetrical and once you establish the axis of the pattern, you can continue analysing the crater further.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You just mentioned the pattern being symmetrical and an axis, on this drawing could you draw what the symmetry would be in the axis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding, when you said symmetry and when you're talking about axis, is it that the symmetry is around the axis on the two sides of the axis and that you have already drawn the axis which comes from the right upper part of this screen and that therefore the symmetry is found on the -- to the left and to the right of -- or at least to the two sides of that axis you've drawn already? Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. The symmetry that I'm talking about is not a hundred per cent symmetry. We cannot claim for a fact that there is the same number of fragments on both sides, but they are more or less symmetrical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- may I put another question. Can we please indicate by an arrow from which side the -- the shell landed or was fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps could the arrow indicate the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- direction of the projectile at impact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In this particular case, the projectile would have come from the right-hand side, and it would have ascended at an angle which would depend on the angle at which it was fired. The descent angle obviously depends on the firing angle. Based on that we carry on all the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, could you please mark an M, the letter M, at the top of this drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And after the witness marks, the Prosecution would tender this as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The M standing for "mortar," we assume, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This impact of a mortar shell. No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document created by the witness in court receives number P930, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, I'd like to do the same exercise with you with respect to an artillery shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the witness could be again provided with a blank screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you could please again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, often -- but that's my understanding, often a mortar is considered to be part of artillery. So an artillery shell and mortar shell seems to confuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, I'd like you to repeat this exercise with an artillery projectile without a stabiliser such as one launched from a cannon or a howitzer. If you could please first on the left-hand side of the screen draw how such an artillery shell would impact and explode on a horizontal surface.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Marks]. This is a simplified representation. When it comes to these shells, unlike with mortars, there are direct firing. They fall under a very acute angle with respect to the surface. Most of the fragments, therefore, can be found in the back behind the axis of the flight. The others are dispersed in the air and they do not hit the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If to the right of this drawing, if you could please draw how that pattern would appear on the ground.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to draw the crater pattern from memory. [Marks]. In very simple terms, most of the fragments would hit behind the crater. As far as I remember, it would be a funnel or a jet-shaped pattern, whereas very small numbers of those fragments may be expected in front of the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please on this pattern draw an arrow that would indicate the direction from which the artillery would arrive. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And if at the top of this drawing would you please write the letter A. I'm just using it for "artillery."

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify once again. Mortars are also artillery pieces. Maybe we can put the letters AR standing for "rotating artillery." Maybe that would explain things better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put another question. On the right side of your drawing you put some lines, uninterrupted lines on the right side of the right drawing. What do they represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, these are some lines that represent the border lines for the density of the jet. They do not exist on any crater. I just use it to delineate the zone where most of the projectile fragments land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was very helpful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I also add my --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If this is rotating artillery, may I suggest we call it RA instead of AR.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution at this time tenders the drawing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any objections, if you want to hear from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document create by the witness in court receives number P931, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P931 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, as a general question, at what -- how would the pattern be affected if the rotating artillery impacted upon a vertical surface? Such as a wall.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: If it were to hit a vertical surface, although I never analysed any such craters, but I did have opportunities to see those on the walls. There would be a higher degree of dispersion of the fragments from all sides of the crater, because the projectile would ascend under a very large angle with respect to the surface. In any case, there would be a more prominent density on the side from which the projectile came, on the side of the descent angle of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how the damage caused by a modified air bomb differs from the damage caused by a mortar or rotating artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, they are intended for different purposes. Air bombs are destructive weapons. They destroyed facilities, and they cause and create large craters on impact. There are fewer fragments because they're not intended for individual impact but for destruction, whether artillery -- whereas artillery projectiles have individual impact. They create smaller craters, and they leave more fragment traces on the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In addition to your participation in on-site investigations, did you perform laboratory analysis of trace evidence recovered from the scenes of explosions?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: We performed laboratory analysis of traces, but not chemical analysis of the materials which were found at explosion sites. We just inspected visually. We measured, and we did comparative analysis with the assets that we had in our department. Obviously, we relied on professional literature when we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 53 of your amalgamated statement, you comment upon a report dated 19 June 1995, which was authored by yourself and Mirza Jamakovic concerning the traces recovered during a shelling incident on Safeta Hadzica Street on 26 May 1995. Did you participate in the on-site investigation of this shelling?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't take part in the investigation on the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P495, page 11 of the B/C/S original and page 10 of the English translation. Your Honours, I am about to go on to another document. I do note the time. It is okay if I break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break now. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, Mr. Lukic, just a very brief survey by the Chamber revealed that at least for a number, I think we came to four now, of the documents you said the witness did not author or had nothing to the investigation, the witness himself says that he either drafted the report or was involved in investigating. So would you please be very precise in the formulation of your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I couldn't find that in the document. Maybe he said "drafted," but I found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if he says that in his statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- his name only on those three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if he -- if he states that he was drafting, although not signing sometimes the report, that of course brings him very close to those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may assist. I'm going to lead a little bit more evidence on this. The initials ES appear in the documents which I'll believe is -- I'll lead some further evidence about what that ES means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from that, Mr. Lukic, of course, before objecting, we would have to look at both the statement and the document and not just the one of the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we have page 11 of the B/C/S and 10 of the English translation of Exhibit P495.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If it could not be broadcast to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, I'd like to return to discussing the shelling on Safeta Hadzica Street. I'd like to direct your attention to another report dated 10 -- if we could please have -- I'd like to draw your attention to another report dated 10 June 1995 concerning the same incident but in relation to the analysis of traces of a projectile that hit the wall of a building on Safeta Hadzica Street. Do you recognise the document before you?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please have the next page of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this next page we see the report was signed by the head of the unit, Mirza Jamakovic. To the left of the signature and the stamp there are the initials ES. Could you please verify if these are your initials and tell us who drafted the analysis described in this report.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are my initials. I drafted this report, and the head of unit, Mirza Jamakovic, was the one who signed every report produced by the unit. So I drafted the report, and I carried out the analysis with assistance of my colleagues. I was not in charge of this case but I did compile a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss your analysis in this report. On the same page you found that the projectile was probably a high explosive 88-millimetre calibre shell. What kind of shell is this?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's a projectile fired from an artillery piece, and it's a rotating projectile. It was most probably fired from a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What do the remarks "4.5 mm klb (n)" represent?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That represents the marking of the projectile that led us to make conclusions based on the analysis of the traces, and this is the way in which projectiles were marked, which indicates that this specific projectile was not produced in the former Yugoslavia, but I think most probably it was made in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How was it that you were able to determine that this was a rotating artillery shell based on the recovered fragments from the projectile?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: After analysing and measuring the fragments retrieved, although we didn't get too many of them, and after analysing all these fragments, we were led to believe that this was probably this specific projectile. We were not 100 per cent sure that it was, in fact, this projectile. However, by process of elimination of all the other known projectiles, based on the measurements and the detailed analysis of the traces, we were led to believe that this projectile is the one as specified in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are there any measurements or observations that you made related to the thickness of the materials recovered which indicated to you that the projectile likely came from a rotating artillery shell as opposed to a mortar?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are measurements. One measures the thickness, which is a dimension which indicates the thickness of the wall or the body of the projectile, and that is one of the elements that led us to believe that this was an artillery projectile, because no other known projectile could have been associated with these specific traces, and all the samples of other projectiles we had on our premises, and we used them for comparison and analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution is finished with this document. We'd like to move on to a different date. Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 10140, page 2 of the B/C/S version only.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, the Prosecution would now like to discuss with you some photographs related to projectile impacts on 16 June 1995. Appearing on the screen before you shortly will be photographs of items found at the scene of a projectile impact near 10 Trg Medjunarodnog Prijateljstva Square. Before we discuss these projectiles, do you know where the square is located?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Trg Medjunarodnog Prijateljstva is in the part of town called Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the top photo, could you please describe the items depicted starting from the item on the far left and continuing to the right. If needed, we can zoom in closer on the photo.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This photo depicts the remnants of rocket motors. On the left-hand side is a piece with seven openings. That's the rear part of the motor, the so-called jet part. During the combustion of fuel, it produces gases which produce thrust for the projectile. In the middle one can see two cylindrical parts. These are also rear parts of rocket motors, and to the left is a piece of metal sheet probably coming from the body of the motor which due to the explosion was deformed, which means that the motor was destroyed and the metal sheet was deformed. In these two middle cylindrical parts, one can see tail-fins of stabilisers that each rocket has.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know what these rockets were used for during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: These rockets were used as a propelling part that consisted of rocket mortars as a propelling device and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer. You said "these rockets were used as a propelling part that consisted of," and then repeat from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a propelling part for modified air bombs that consisted of the propelling device, i.e., rocket engines that propelled the entire improvised device and an aerial bomb itself which served as a warhead, i.e., as an explosive device which exploded on impact and inflicted huge damage, destruction, and loss of life. These two parts were technically welded to one another by an adaptor in the shape of a plate in order to make it compact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the clarity of the record I will put one question to the witness. In one of your previous answers you said -- this is at least what was translated to us: "To the left is a piece of metal sheet probably coming from the body of the motor." Did you really say to the left or to the right? You explained which because of the explosion was deformed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the piece on the far right of irregular shape. It's a piece of metal sheet originating from the rocket motor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this correction of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You also referred to the stabiliser part. Could you tell us exactly where you find this stabilising part of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this photograph there are a few fins of the stabiliser. To the left where you have this piece with jet openings, you can see two fins which are not open. And you can also see stabiliser fins each on the two central pieces, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that on the central pieces the -- the shapes for both of them to the right lower part, slightly bended, are these the stabiliser elements attached to the -- to the rocket part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have one final question on this. The fact that there are stabilisers which apparently are movable, does that mean that these projectiles do not rotate in the air but are supposed to fly without rotation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we speak about a rocket, a rocket does not rotate and neither did this modified device made up of an air bomb and rocket motors. Only I would like to add that probably these fins never opened in this modified device. They were fixed, because there was no need for them to stabilise the flight of this specific projectile. I think that they were fixed, and therefore it was impossible for them to open. I think that we discovered that they were fixed in a way in order to prevent them from opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could we zoom out again so that we have this together with the other. May I take it that what we see close to the number 1 on the picture above is the same -- that is, the seven holes part of this -- the part of the projectile with the seven holes, that that is the same as we see on the lower part lying flat to the left of the two others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I presume that is the case. I didn't make the photograph. However, these jet parts are found in the central pieces as well, only you cannot see them in this photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if we zoom in on the lower photograph we might see it, because it's taken from a different angle, and even a smaller part -- yes. We see a similar seven holes at least in the middle one as we saw earlier to the left. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 10140 into evidence, the photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10140 receives number P932, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 10394, page 9 of the uploaded B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, in paragraphs 59 and 60 of your amalgamated statement you authenticate a report concerning a projectile that landed at Cobanija Street on the same date, 16 June 1995. Coming before you will be some photos of items recovered at the location of this impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the numbers and the page of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's -- I have paragraphs 59 and 60 of the amalgamated statement. It's related to the Cobanija Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could start with the top photograph. If you could tell us which items are depicted in this photo.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The top photo shows several pieces of damaged and distorted metal sheet. These fragments are parts of rocket motor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And directing your attention to the bottom photo. Could you tell us what are the items that we see.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This photo shows parts of the rear end of the rocket motor. The one to the very left is the stabiliser axis, only there is no stabiliser that can be seen on this particular piece because it probably fell off during the explosion. The other two parts came from the rear end of the rocket motor where the jets are, only they are damaged and distorted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 10394 into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object to this one and maybe to MFI this, and during the cross-examination we will show why we object to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's fine. I can -- depending on what happens, I can re-tender in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although usually objections are formulated and reasoned when admission is sought, but it maybe very practical to deal with it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can say now, because maybe this gentleman should be asked whether he composed the document or not and what's his knowledge about that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see what he exactly says about that so that we are prepared --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because I find some other people's names on this document, not his.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- if I could get to the -- the reports are authored by a colleague of his. He indicates and authenticates the signature related to the reports in this statement. With respect to the witness's evidence, the witness has knowledge and has been able to provide us with relevant knowledge concerning the items that are in these photographs. This is the same date as scheduled incident G15, so the impact of modified air bombs or rockets are directly relevant to this case. We ask that the photos be admitted at this time. That's the only basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry maybe there is a misunderstanding on my part. If that's only the photos, we do not object, but I thought we are talking about the whole paragraph, 59, and about the document inside. I mentioned that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that there may be two matters to be distinguished. The first one, the authentication of the report and the signature by this witness which is apart from the content of the report. Now, each of these separate issues would already justify admission into evidence although the probative value then to be discussed as to what the witness could tell us about the content of the report, therefore it seems to go rather to whether the content of the report also provides probative value or whether it's primarily or exclusively the authentication of the document and the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's that -- just the authentication, then probably he can recognise that signatures of his colleagues, but about the content --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But can we clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have it MFI'd, I think, for whatever purpose, if only for authentication purposes that might already justify admission, but let's wait and see what you come up in cross-examination. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have a clarification? The document 65 ter 10394, does that contain the report or only these two photographs on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Two separate materials, Your Honour. There's a report and then there are the photographs I've shown the witness. So I'm asking for the admission based on the testimony of this witness at this stage right now of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the photographs only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10394 receives number P933, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, in our 92 ter motion for the witness we sought leave to add photographs. We're requesting permission to show these photographs to the witness at this stage of the examination. They have been uploaded under 65 ter 28670.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I hear of no objections of the photographs to be shown to the witness to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections at this moment for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would also mean that you do not object against adding them to the 65 ter list because they now become potential evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Leave is granted to add them to the 65 ter list. You may show the photographs to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could please have page 4 of 65 ter 28670.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, directing your attention to the bottom photo before you. Do you recognise the location as depicted?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a factory -- or, rather, the Ilijas ironworks, and Ilijas is a place near Sarajevo. Throughout the war, Ilijas was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where -- where is the Ilijas ironworks factory in relation to the centre of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: It is not in Sarajevo. Before the war Ilijas used to be one of Sarajevo municipalities, but nowadays Ilijas is a small settlement some 20 to 30 kilometres away from Sarajevo. This means that Ilijas is actually on the road towards Zenica. It is not part of the city of Sarajevo at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And when you say it's 30 kilometres away from Sarajevo, is it 30 kilometres to the north or is it 30 kilometres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, the Chamber has maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was just trying to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is Ilijas and the town or the -- of Ilijas, then there should be no problem to find it apart from that you could agree on where Ilijas is, but I don't think there is much dispute about it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless the specific location of the factory is some relevance. Then, of course, I'm not keeping you from exploring that, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know when these photographs were taken, approximately?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I know when they were taken. They were taken after the signing of the Dayton Accords. During the reintegration process of the municipalities and the parts that had been under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, after the Dayton Accords they were given to the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those parts were reintegrated and our department was one of the first that entered those reintegrated areas in order to make sure that other persons could enter, to make sure that there were no explosions, that mines were cleared if they were found, as well as to carry out inspections at requests by companies and individuals if they suspected that explosives and explosive devices could be found at certain places. At the time when those photos were taken I was not in Ilijas myself, but one of the teams from my department were given the task, and during the integration process and during the inspection of the area they took those photos. Somebody from the team, I don't know if that person was from my department, but in any case, those photos were taken in early 1996 by a team member, who did not necessarily have to be a member of my department.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention to the top photo now. Could you please tell us what is depicted.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: It depicts bombs as they are stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know what type of bombs these are?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what type it is, but in any case, they are air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, directing your attention to the bottom photo, do you know what is depicted?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: The bottom photo depicts 200-litre barrels filled with explosives. On the left-hand side is a barrel without any additions, probably filled with explosives, which we can't see, but we can see wheels belonging to cargo vehicles which were attached to the barrels which in turn made the barrels for transport or for lowering them downhill. Actually, that's how they were used to bomb settled areas. Barrels would be rolled down the hill. The explosives would be activated by slow fuses, and when the slow fuses burnt down completely, the explosives would be activated and the barrel would explode. During the war, that happened on the slopes above Sarajevo in the settlement called Bistrik. I myself wasn't there, but I heard that residential buildings and other facilities were destroyed in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28670 into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28670 receives number P934, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And if we could just clarify one thing with respect to these photos. Does your signature appear at the bottom of each page of these photographs and a date when you signed it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it on this page. I don't know whether my signature is on all pages. In my previous testimonies, I offered those photos because I had them at my disposal, and I did that on the date depicted in the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, before we do so, before I start being puzzled about it, could you tell me what -- whether there's any difference between the photograph on the first page of this document and the lower photograph on the last page, that is page 6 of this document? They seem so much the same to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that there's multiple photos that depict --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if that's the case, I'll not try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There's also multiple photos of the -- what the witness has described to be the aerial bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There are slight differences in those, though, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, I'd like to turn to a different topic. During the course of your investigations, did you become familiar with markings on fragments of mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What type of markings would you find on the remaining fragments of a mortar shell after the shelling?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: A mitigating circumstance was when one found markings on a fragment. However, when it came to mortar shells, whenever a stabiliser was found, and it was found in most cases, on the lower end the primary charged -- charge contained markings. According to professional literature which dealt with the markings of artillery ammunition, things were described in detail, and we used that. The markings consisted of the designation of the producer, the year of production, the series in that year when that device was manufactured. The letter markings indicated the producer, the manufacturer. The former JNA -- or, rather, its purpose industry had well-established markings for the companies that produced explosives. For example, SRB denoted --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, sorry to cut you off. We will go through some examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the Prosecution at this time could please display an amended version that we sought leave to amend in our 92 ter motion of 65 ter 19024. We have uploaded it as 19024A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is part of the motion. Mr. Lukic, no objection against it being used at this point in time. Therefore, the amended version is now part of your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could please have page 2 of 65 ter 19024A.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, in the previous answer that you just gave, you stated that you used professional literature which dealt with markings of artillery ammunition. Do you recognise the document before you as one of those pieces of literature?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was one of the basic books which dealt with markings. This is a textbook which was used by the students of the military academy in Zagreb. It was an institution of higher military learning in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 4 of both versions of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, I'd like to direct your attention to the centre of the page, the part entitled "Designation for an explosive-filled series of projectiles." Could you please explain to us what kind of projectiles does this section relate to?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This relates to all projectiles filled with some explosive, either gunpowder or something else, some other explosive agent. And this could be either primary charge or the casings of artillery projectiles including mortars, and that's when they were filled with explosives. This is what is described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There's reference to a table 11 in this section. I'd like to take you to that table right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could please go two pages forward in both versions. I'm sorry, Your Honour, did you have a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I see it already. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could actually go one page back. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the far left column of this table is an explanation for the designations for projectiles produced in the former Yugoslavia. I'd like to draw your attention to the example provided for KB 5701. Could you just take us through this example and explain what these markings mean.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, there are two parts of a designation, the letter part and the numerical part. KB is in Cyrillic, and it stands for Krusik Valjevo. It's actually not KB but KV, but in Cyrillic. Krusik Valjevo. Fifty-seven, the first two digits in the numerical part, represent the year when the projectile was filled with charge. The rest of the numerical part designate the series in the year when that projectile was filled with the charge, because explosives were filled in batches, in series, and each of the batches, each of the series, bore its own series number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to take you to another example, in paragraph 48 of your amalgamated statement, you comment on a portion of a report related to a 120-millimetre mortar projectile that landed on Asikovac Street on the date of 22 May 1995. You indicate that the marking KB 9502 is short for Krusik Valjevo in Serbia and the year of manufacture is 1995 as part of the second series. Do I understand correctly that these markings indicate that the mortar was manufactured in Serbia during the same year that it impacted upon this location?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the primary charge. This means that the primary charge was manufactured and inserted in the casing in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just so we're clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At lines 12 at page 42, starting from line 12, the witness says: "57, the first two digits in the numerical part, represent the year when the projectile was filled with charge." And then he says: "The rest of the numerical part designate the series in the year when that projectile was filled with the charge."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand the distinction between those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that it would be best to just ask the witness to -- if he could further clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The numerical part -- or, rather, the letter part indicates the manufacturer, i.e., the company when all the works were done. The first part of the numerical part designates the year of production. If it's 57, that means the year 1957. In the year 1957, there were several series or several batches when explosives were filled. It was not done continuously. There were interruptions between the series, and each of the series in the year was designated by a different number, a different serial number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one additional question in relation to this. You said filling was the primary charge which was filled. Do I understand that you are talking about the primary charge as the explosive charge? So not a charge which served for propelling the projectile, but the charge with explosives which were to explode upon impact? Is that how I have to understand your primary charge, use of that term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about the primary propellant, the gunpowder which is inserted in the -- in the propellant part. In this particular case, we did not find a fragment with the designation that would indicate as to when the charge was filled in the casing of the explosive device. Maybe the casing was manufactured in 1994 or perhaps even earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are here talking about the propelling charge only, and that is what these designations stand for, that is the -- where, what year, what batch, or am I -- let me just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, yes, that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So all the numbers here, et cetera, we're talking about are exclusively about the propelling charge of the projectile, not the exploding part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we're talking about the markings, this relates to the primary charge, and in general terms we're talking about two different charges, the charge in the casing and the propelling charge. When you say "filling," it applies to both cases, the case of filling the shell casing with explosive or the propellant charge, and the designations are the same for both, but it all depended on the manufacturers. The markings will not be identical for different manufacturers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So similar designation could be found on the body of the shell and on the propelling part and would be interpreted in a similar way but might be different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. If a primary charge was manufactured in one company, that does not necessarily mean that the projectile, the casing itself, was made in the same factory. That may well be the case, but it doesn't have to be. In any case, whatever markings are found, they indicate the manufacturer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, today at page 6, lines 11 and 12, after I asked you to clarify what you meant by "primary charge," you stated: "The primary charge is on the lower side of the stabiliser." Is this the location where you would find the markings that you've described?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your amalgamated statement, you comment on a number of other reports related to other shelling incidents in 1995. Six of these reports note markings on 120-millimetre stabilisers as KB 9309, KB 9402, two stabilisers recovered nine days apart had the markings KB 9501, and two stabilisers recovered ten days apart had the markings KB 9503. From these markings can you confirm that all of these primary charges were manufactured in Serbia at Krusik between 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, the letters should be KB in Cyrillic standing for KV, not KD, at least that's what I heard in the interpretation. So KD is wrong. It should be KB in Cyrillic standing for KV. In other words, all of these primary charges were completed. They were manufactured and completed in the Krusik Valjevo factory from 1993 to 1995. This is what I can interpret from the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 10924A into evidence as a public exhibit. For the Chamber's reference, there are diagrams that are also uploaded as part of this. If you saw in the earlier paragraph, there was references to these images and they are also attached. If -- with Your Honours' leave, too, I can take the witness through another report if the Chamber and Mr. Lukic would like, but I would tender also -- 65 ter 15696A is another report authored by the witness concerning the shelling on 2 July 1995 in Novi Grad where the markings on the primary charge were found to be KB 9404. We are offering this report to show a consistent pattern in the use of certain types of projectiles during shellings on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19024A receives number P935, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we also have 15696A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P936, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P935 and P936 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders the witness. No further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, perhaps the best would be to take the break first before you start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will take another break. Would you please follow the usher, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
